story.story:
In December 1975 the Royal Newfoundland Constabulary opened an investigation into abuse at the Mount Cashel orphanage in St John's, and the police chief closed it nine days later. In 1976 the Justice Department ordered the police report rewritten, and in 1977 the Deputy Minister of Justice said further action was not warranted. Nothing more was done until 1989, when the Hughes Inquiry, a royal commission with the power to require evidence, was set up to examine how Newfoundland's criminal justice system had responded. It found that officials had transferred offenders and covered up abuse. Eleven Christian Brothers, members of a Catholic religious order, were convicted, and in 1996 Newfoundland paid C$11.5 million in compensation.

The federal government funded residential schools, run by churches, to assimilate First Nations, Métis and Inuit children, and about 150,000 children attended them. Under a settlement reached in 2007, tens of thousands of claims of sexual and serious physical abuse at the schools were compensated.

Two priests of the Oblates of Mary Immaculate, a Catholic missionary order, who had worked in Nunavut, were accused of abusing Inuit children and moved to Europe. Eric Dejaeger had already served five years in the early 1990s for abusing children in Baker Lake. In 1995, when he was about to be charged over abuse in Igloolik, he fled to Belgium, and Oblate officials later acknowledged they knew he was leaving. He lived in Oblate houses there for 16 years despite an international warrant. After he was returned in 2011 he was sentenced to 19 years for 32 sex crimes against Inuit children. Johannes Rivoire, a French Oblate, left for France in January 1993. Canada issued a warrant for him in 1998 over abuse of Inuit children, and in 2022 issued another and asked France to extradite him, which the French authorities refused. A 2024 review commissioned by the Oblates concluded that he had assaulted six children. He died in France that year without trial.

Where an accused priest left Canada, whether he was ever tried depended on whether the country he went to would send him back.

story.story:
Complaints about Jimmy Savile, one of the BBC's best-known presenters, reached the police from 1958. Two police investigations in his lifetime produced no charges, Surrey Police dropped an inquiry in 2007–09, and in December 2011 the BBC shelved a report about him by its own Newsnight programme. In October 2012 London's Metropolitan Police opened Operation Yewtree, and in 2013 it recorded 214 crimes by him. Later inquiries found 72 victims linked to the BBC and victims aged 5 to 75 in hospitals of the state health service.

In Rotherham, children's-home managers and youth workers reported the sexual exploitation of children from the early-to-mid 1990s, and the researcher Angie Heal warned officials from 2002 to 2007. A rape reported in 2001 ended with the suspect released without charge, and action against the abusers began only in 2010. An independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited in the town between 1997 and 2013, and called the failures of the council and the police 'blatant'. The National Crime Agency, the national agency for serious crime, then took over the case; it has identified about 1,150 potential victims, and 39 people have been convicted. In Oxfordshire a review in 2015 found that police did not believe the girls and treated them as if they had chosen their situation.

Medomsley Detention Centre in County Durham held young male offenders from 1961 to 1988. Neville Husband, the officer who ran its kitchens, was convicted of sexual offences in 2003 and 2005, and eight former staff were jailed. In November 2025 the Prisons and Probation Ombudsman, the independent investigator of complaints about prisons, found that what the Prison Service, the police and the Home Office knew of the abuse had been 'ignored and dismissed'.

From June 2026 people in England and Wales who were abused as children can sue however long ago the abuse happened, unless the defendant shows a fair trial is impossible. The National Crime Agency is now investigating allegations that former South Yorkshire Police officers abused children, and no finding has yet been made.

story.story:
In December 2006 UNICEF and Kenya's Ministry of Home Affairs published a joint study of four beach resort areas. It found that up to 30 percent of girls aged 12 to 18 living there were involved in casual sex work, and that two to three thousand children were in full-time commercial sex. Kenyans made up 38 percent of the buyers, and tourists from Italy, Germany and Switzerland 44 percent. Vice President Moody Awori accepted the findings and said the police and local communities had failed to enforce the law.

The trade continued and moved. The 2025 US State Department trafficking report cites a 2023 study by a non-governmental organisation estimating that more than 2,000 children were sold for sex in Kilifi and Kwale counties, and says the abuse there is moving from hotels into private villas and holiday homes. The report also describes rings bringing underage girls from Uganda's Karamoja region to Nairobi, and notes concerns that officials take part, with no action reported against any of them.

Babies and young children were also bought and sold in Nairobi. In 2020 a year-long BBC investigation found children taken from homeless mothers in Nairobi and sold for about £350 to £550, A clinical social worker at Mama Lucy Kibaki Hospital, a government hospital, sold an abandoned two-week-old boy to undercover reporters for 300,000 shillings. The BBC said he appeared to keep his job.

Children were also abused in homes funded from abroad. At Nyumbani, a Nairobi home for children with HIV that drew large donations from the United States, a 2021 investigation by USAID, the US government's aid agency, found claims credible that volunteers, caregivers and other children had raped children there. A USAID memo said the co-founder had known of abuse allegations since 2006 and had failed to respond. The co-founder stepped down in 2023 after questions from the Washington Post.

Since the 2006 study no Kenyan government inquiry appears in the records gathered for this map, and what is known has come from foreign governments, charities and journalists. The most recent describe children still sold for sex on the coast.

story.story:
In January 1980 the Archdiocese of Munich, then led by Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger, accepted Fr Peter Hullermann from the Diocese of Essen for therapy after Essen had suspended him over the abuse of a boy. Munich gave him parish work, and he abused minors again. He was convicted in 1986, given a suspended sentence, and kept serving in Bavarian parishes until 2010. Later university studies of dioceses found such transfers common. In Münster, historians found in 2022 that at least 610 minors had been abused by 196 clerics since 1945, estimated the real number of victims at eight to ten times higher, and found that bishops usually transferred accused priests.

Youth offices, the public agencies responsible for children in care, also placed children with abusers. From the late 1960s Berlin's youth authorities, on the advice of the psychologist Helmut Kentler, placed boys in foster care with men known to be paedophiles, a practice that continued into the 2000s. In Lügde, a youth office placed a foster daughter with Andreas V., who lived at a campsite. Police received two tips about him in 2016 and did not act. In 2019 he and a second man were convicted of abusing 32 children there between 1998 and 2018, and a state parliamentary inquiry found they could have been stopped two years earlier.

The legal deadlines for bringing cases, called statutes of limitations, also protected offenders. At the Odenwaldschule, a boarding school, former pupils came forward in 1998, and prosecutors dropped the case because the deadline had passed. In 2013 the Bundestag, the federal parliament, extended the deadline for civil claims from 3 to 30 years, but not for claims that had already expired.

Abuse material is also hosted and traded from Germany. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity, acted on 18,401 internet addresses of abuse material on German servers. In 2021 German police took down Boystown, a platform run by German administrators that had 400,000 registered users.

Church and state inquiries have now counted many victims of abuse in German institutions, and many older cases can no longer be taken to court.

story.story:
Mainly from 1930 to 1981, Swiss cantonal and municipal authorities sent more than 60,000 people to about 650 institutions without any court order, a practice known as administrative detention. They included the Verdingkinder, children placed with farmers as indentured labourers. Those held were abused physically, psychologically and sexually. A programme of the foundation Pro Juventute, backed by federal authorities, removed about 590 Yenish children from their families.

The Swiss government apologised in 2010. A 2016 law gave victims of these compulsory measures a "solidarity contribution" of CHF 25,000, and in 2019 an independent expert commission published its final report. In February 2025 the government recognised the Pro Juventute programme as a crime against humanity.

From the 1970s, Swiss families adopted children from abroad, including 1,111 from South Korea between 1968 and 1997 and others from Sri Lanka, India and Tibet. Swiss authorities realised that many children had been wrongly presented as orphans, and that placements were driven by money and linked to organised child trafficking. Decisions often rested on incomplete or falsified documents. After pressure from adoptees' groups such as Back to the Roots, parliament commissioned a study in 2018. The Federal Council, the Swiss government, acknowledged the authorities' failures in 2020 and 2023, and at the end of 2024 recommended a general ban on intercountry adoption.

In 2023 historians at the University of Zurich, in a study paid for by the Swiss Bishops' Conference and religious orders, documented 1,002 cases of sexual abuse in the Catholic Church since 1950, with 510 accused people and 921 victims. Of the documents, 74 percent concerned minors, and about 30 percent of cases took place in Catholic children's homes, schools and boarding schools. The researchers found that church law was hardly ever applied and that many cases were kept secret.

The state has apologised to and paid victims of the forced placements, and the government has proposed ending intercountry adoption. The church researchers said the cases they found were only a small part of the total, so the full number of children abused in the church is not known.

story.story:
From 1973 to 1983 Joseph Marshall and his wife ran Knottfield, a children's home owned by the Isle of Man Government. In 1992 Marshall was convicted of 13 offences relating to Knottfield.

In 2018 a scrutiny committee of Tynwald, the island's parliament, chaired by David Cretney, reported on the "horrific physical, emotional and sexual abuse" Marshall had committed at the home and made 11 recommendations. The report was withdrawn while a new criminal case against Marshall went ahead. In April 2022 he was jailed for six years for sexually abusing two boys at Knottfield. On 16 January 2023 the Isle of Man Government apologised for mistakes that had contributed to the abuse and said it supported all 11 recommendations.

The committee's report covers one home. No wider official inquiry into abuse in the island's institutions is recorded, so how far the failures at Knottfield happened elsewhere is not known.

story.story:
In March 2010 the Catholic Church in the Netherlands set up a commission led by the former minister Wim Deetman to investigate abuse by its clergy. Its report in December 2011 identified at least 800 priests, monks and other members of religious orders who had abused children between 1945 and 1985, 105 of them still alive, and estimated that 10,000 to 20,000 minors had been abused. It found that bishops and church officials had known and followed a policy of "not hanging out the dirty washing", that is, of avoiding scandal.

Inquiries into the state's own care system followed. In 2012 a commission chaired by Rieke Samson, a former senior prosecutor, received 800 claims of sexual abuse of children placed in care since 1945, 65% about children's homes and 30% about foster families, and passed 42 files to the public prosecutor. In 2019 a commission led by Micha de Winter found that a considerable share of children in youth care since 1945 had not been protected from physical, psychological and sexual violence, and that the government had done too little.

The Netherlands also received children from abroad for adoption, including 4,099 from South Korea between 1969 and 2003 and about 4,000 from Sri Lanka in the 1980s. In February 2021 a government committee chaired by Tjibbe Joustra found serious violations in adoptions from 1967 to 1997/98 and concluded that the Dutch government had for decades failed to prevent them. The government suspended all intercountry adoption that month, and in May 2024 announced that citizens would no longer be allowed to adopt from abroad.

Dutch servers have hosted much of the world's abuse material. In 2018, 47% of the material acted on by the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds such images, was hosted in the Netherlands. In 2025 the share was 11%, or 33,788 internet addresses.

The church, state care and foreign adoption have each been examined by an inquiry, and adoption from abroad is being ended. The country's National Rapporteur reported exploitation cases rising from 868 in 2023 to 944 in 2024, with more teenage victims.

story.story:
Between 1971 and 1991, Fr Bernard Preynat, a priest in Lyon, was accused of abusing about 80 Boy Scouts. Many of the cases had passed the statute of limitations, the legal deadline for bringing a case, so he was tried for assaults on 10 minors from 1986 to 1991, and in March 2020 a Lyon court sentenced him to five years in prison.

In November 2018 the French bishops set up the Independent Commission on Sexual Abuse in the Church (CIASE). It surveyed the general population as well as church archives. Its report in October 2021 estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as minors by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, and about 330,000 if lay people working for the church were included. It called the causes systemic.

In 2004 the FBI traced a surgeon in western France, Joël Le Scouarnec, downloading abuse images. In 2005 he received a four-month suspended sentence, and prosecutors did not tell the medical authorities. A warning to the health ministry in 2007 brought no action, and a hospital hired him in 2008 knowing of the conviction. At his second trial he admitted abusing 299 victims between 1989 and 2014, mostly patients, many under anaesthesia, more than 250 of them under 15. In May 2025 he was sentenced to the maximum of 20 years.

In 2021 the government created CIIVISE, a commission on incest and sexual violence against children. In November 2023 it estimated that 160,000 children suffer sexual violence in France each year. Under the law, rape of a minor can be prosecuted until 30 years after the victim turns 18; CIIVISE asked for the deadline to be removed, which had not been adopted when it reported. In April 2025 a parliamentary inquiry estimated that about 15,000 children in the care of the state child welfare services, the ASE, are exploited in prostitution.

France now has national estimates of abuse in the church and in families, and its parliament has found children in state care exploited in prostitution. The deadline for prosecuting rape of a minor still applies.

story.story:
In 1974 the bishop of the Diocese of Lafayette, in Louisiana, made Fr Gilbert Gauthe a Boy Scout chaplain despite allegations that he had abused altar boys. In 1976 Gauthe was sent for therapy and then returned to work. He later admitted abusing 37 children, and in 1985 he pleaded guilty and was sentenced to 20 years. His was the first widely publicised prosecution of a priest for abuse in the United States.

At Pennsylvania State University, a 1998 report to the university police about the assistant football coach Jerry Sandusky was not prosecuted. In 2001 a graduate assistant's report of seeing Sandusky with a boy in a shower went to the coach Joe Paterno and university officials, who did not tell the police. Sandusky was convicted in 2012 of abusing 10 boys, and in 2017 the athletic director, a vice-president and the university's president were convicted of child endangerment. Gymnasts complained about the team doctor Larry Nassar from 1997. The FBI was told in July 2015 but did not act, and the Justice Department's internal watchdog found that at least 70 more athletes were abused between the reports to the FBI and his arrest. By his final hearing, 265 victims had been identified.

In 2005 Palm Beach police in Florida investigated the financier Jeffrey Epstein and identified about 35 girls, but a state grand jury, a panel of citizens that decides on charges, returned only a single count of soliciting prostitution. In 2007 the federal prosecutor's office under Alexander Acosta agreed not to bring federal charges against Epstein and several suspected co-conspirators and kept the agreement from the victims. Epstein served 13 months of an 18-month state sentence.

When states proposed lengthening the legal deadlines for suing over childhood abuse, Catholic organisations, insurers and the Scouts lobbied against the changes. At least 41 Catholic dioceses and orders, the Boy Scouts of America and USA Gymnastics filed for bankruptcy facing abuse claims.

No national inquiry into abuse in American institutions has been held; the investigations have been by state attorneys general and grand juries, or commissioned by the church.

story.story:
In 1979 Fettes College, a school in Edinburgh, dismissed the teacher Iain Wares but gave him a glowing reference. He went on to teach in South Africa, where he later abused children; South Africa approved his extradition to Scotland, which he was still contesting in 2025. Fr Georg Kerkhoff, a German priest with abuse cases pending at home, worked in South Africa and was tried there for abusing boys at a 2008 camp before being extradited and jailed in Germany in 2015.

The British barrister John Smyth moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, after a 1982 internal report of the Iwerne Trust, the evangelical charity he had chaired, described how he beat boys he met at its camps. Refused re-entry to Zimbabwe, he moved to South Africa in 2001. The Makin Review, published in England in 2024, found it highly likely that he kept abusing until his death in Cape Town in 2018. He was never charged anywhere.

In June 2026 the South African Human Rights Commission described sexual violence in schools as systemic. It recorded 826 complaints of sexual misconduct made between 2021 and 2025 to the South African Council for Educators, the body that registers teachers. It found that a teacher struck off by the council is not automatically added to the register of people barred from working with children, and that 10,748 convicted offenders had not been entered on the National Register for Sex Offenders.

The 2025 US State Department trafficking report says traffickers recruit children from rural areas and sell them for sex in Gauteng and Western Cape, that brothel owners use drugs to control them, that some parents sell their own children, and that low-level corruption and complicity among officials continued.

In the case of Timothy Omotoso, first reported in 2017, mistrial motions and recusals delayed the trial for eight years, and a whistleblower, Pamela Mabini, was shot dead in March 2025, weeks before the verdict.

Because of the gaps the commission found, teachers removed for sexual misconduct and convicted sex offenders may be missing from the registers meant to keep them away from South African children.

story.story:
In 2018 the Bihar state government asked Koshish, a unit of the Tata Institute of Social Sciences, to audit 110 children's homes funded by its social welfare department. The audit, submitted in April 2018, graded a girls' home in Muzaffarpur, run by the organisation of Brajesh Thakur, a politically connected man, as criminal negligence, and raised abuse at 14 other homes. Police registered a case on 31 May 2018, and medical examinations indicated that 34 girls, most of them children, had been sexually abused. Bihar's social welfare minister, Manju Verma, resigned. Because the accused were influential in Bihar, the Supreme Court moved the trial to Delhi, where in January 2020 a court convicted Thakur and 18 others. In Deoria, in Uttar Pradesh, police rescued 24 girls from a shelter in 2018; the state minister said the charity's recognition and funds had been withdrawn a year earlier, and the home had kept operating.

Political status also delayed a case against a legislator. In Unnao, a member of the Uttar Pradesh legislature, Kuldeep Singh Sengar, raped a girl in 2017. Her father died in police custody, and Sengar was arrested only after the Allahabad High Court ordered it in 2018. He was convicted in 2019 and sentenced to life.

India also sent 12,511 children abroad for adoption between 2003 and 2022. In 2001 police in Andhra Pradesh exposed a home that had earned Rs 3.33 crore from foreign adoptions, mainly to the United States; in 2005 ten people were sentenced, and the state barred private agencies from placing children.

The US State Department's 2025 report says traffickers bring significant numbers of Nepali and Bangladeshi women and girls into India for sex. In Kolkata in 2015, six young women freed from brothels all carried false adult identity papers, which the charity International Justice Mission said traffickers issue to underage girls.

India has held no national inquiry into abuse in institutions, and Childlight found no representative survey data on online exploitation for South Asia. Its convictions have come from state audits and single cases, and the national scale is unknown.

story.story:
When Clark Air Base, a US military base in Angeles City north of Manila, closed in 1992, the bars around it lost the American soldiers who had been their customers. The same year Manila's mayor, Alfredo Lim, began closing Ermita, the city's main sex-industry district, and many of its businesses moved to Angeles City and took up foreign tourists as customers. In 2025 the US State Department's trafficking report still named Angeles City among the places where sex trafficking frequently occurs. It said most foreign offenders come from Australia, Japan, New Zealand, Britain and the United States, and many are already convicted or charged sex offenders at home.

From 2006 the charity International Justice Mission (IJM) worked with police in several Philippine cities, and by 2016 the number of children trafficked for sex in bars and other establishments there had fallen by 79 to 86 percent. Over 2014 to 2017 the number of Philippine internet addresses used each month for child sexual exploitation grew more than twelvefold. Parents, relatives or neighbours were paid by buyers abroad to abuse children in front of a webcam. Because the buyers were abroad, 64 percent of the cases taken up by the police anti-trafficking unit in 2017 began with a referral from a foreign police force. In 2020 the Australian bank Westpac agreed to a A$1.3 billion penalty for breaking money-laundering law, including failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation in the Philippines. In 2024 Europol, the EU police agency, examined chats between about 12,000 buyer accounts and 100 sellers in the Philippines, gathered over 12 years, and sent leads on 197 buyers to 24 countries.

In 2002 the Catholic bishops apologised and said about 200 of the country's 7,000 priests had committed sexual misconduct over two decades. No national inquiry into abuse in church or state institutions has been found.

IJM estimated that 1 in every 100 children in the Philippines was a victim of online sexual exploitation in 2022. The people paying for it live mostly in a few wealthy countries, so finding them depends on police and banks there.

story.story:
In 1966, under Nicolae Ceaușescu, Romania banned abortion by Decree 770, and many of the children born in the following years were abandoned in state institutions. There they were neglected, sedated, and physically and sexually abused; abuse was reported to be common at the children's psychiatric hospital in Siret. After Ceaușescu fell in 1989, television showed about 100,000 children in Romanian orphanages, and foreign families began adopting them in large numbers. Private agencies charged €7,500 to €25,000 per child, and the system soon became corrupt. The United States alone issued 5,285 visas to children adopted from Romania between 1994 and 2008.

Romania tried several times to stop the trade. It halted adoptions in 1991 and outlawed selling babies, imposed a temporary ban in 2001 after a government commission found that middlemen and officials had taken the money, and in June 2004, under pressure from the European Union, banned foreign adoption except by grandparents. In 2006 there were no intercountry adoptions.

Girls from Romania continued to be sent abroad by other means. From 2009 one criminal group used the "loverboy" method, in which a man pretends to be in love with a vulnerable girl. The group exploited girls in prostitution in Romania until they turned 18 and then moved them to Britain, Ireland and Germany. Romanian and British investigators working together arrested 21 members in 2020. In its 2025 report the US State Department said most identified victims of trafficking from Romania are women and girls exploited at home or in Western Europe. It also said children in state institutions, particularly girls in homes for people with disabilities, are at risk of sex trafficking. Romanian courts convicted 161 traffickers in 2024.

Romania also hosted 21,188 web addresses with abuse material removed by the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity, in 2025, 7 percent of the total.

Foreign adoption from Romania has been closed since 2004. Children still live in state institutions, where girls are at risk from traffickers and some staff are alleged to have been complicit or negligent.

story.story:
In 1992 and 1993 the UN Transitional Authority in Cambodia (UNTAC), a UN mission of about 22,000 personnel, was based in the country. Its arrival was followed by a sharp rise in prostitution, from an estimated 6,000 to more than 25,000 sex workers in two years, and by abuse of Cambodian women and girls. The UN kept no thorough record of allegations at the time.

Svay Pak, a fishing village on the outskirts of Phnom Penh, became a place where foreign men bought sex with children, most of them ethnic Vietnamese girls, many sold by poor families. Reports in 2002 described the trade there as driven by Western sex tourists who had come after Thailand cracked down on child prostitution. On 22 January 2003 police raided the brothels after advertising the raid in advance. Almost all the children had been moved, and no pimps or clients were arrested. Local authorities had been extorting money from the brothel owners. The government closed the Svay Pak brothels in 2005, and the trade moved to massage parlours and karaoke bars. In 2017 ABC News reported that survey estimates of the share of minors among Cambodia's sex workers had fallen from nearly 35 percent to 1 to 2 percent.

Cambodian children were also sent abroad for adoption. The American facilitator Lauryn Galindo arranged about 800 adoptions for US families from 1997 to 2001, more than half of all Cambodian adoptions, and the US government said her business paid Cambodian mothers for babies. The US suspended adoptions from Cambodia in late 2001. In 2004 Galindo pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit visa fraud and money laundering, admitting she had falsified documents; she denied trafficking.

The 2025 US trafficking report said Cambodian and foreign men still sexually exploit children in the tourism industry, and that children as young as 13 are exploited in brothels to pay family debts.

The sale of children moved out of open brothels into less visible places. The same 2025 report said complicity by officials, including at senior levels, still prevents effective law enforcement.

story.story:
In 2008 the Vatican sent the Polish archbishop Józef Wesołowski to the Dominican Republic as its nuncio, the Vatican's ambassador. In August 2013, amid allegations that he was abusing minors, the Vatican recalled him to Rome, and in September Dominican prosecutors opened a criminal investigation. Once he was in the Vatican he was out of reach of Dominican courts, and the Vatican later told Polish prosecutors that its law did not allow him to be extradited. A church tribunal found him guilty and he was dismissed from the priesthood in 2014. In 2015 a Vatican prosecutor charged him with abusing children in the Dominican Republic between 2008 and 2013 and with possessing abuse images, but he was found dead in August 2015, before the trial.

A Polish priest who had worked in the Dominican Republic, Fr Wojciech Gil, was suspended in May 2013 and returned to Poland, which has no extradition treaty with the Dominican Republic. Polish police arrested him in 2014 using Dominican evidence, and in 2015 a Polish court sentenced him to seven years for abusing six minors in the Dominican Republic and two in Poland.

Children are also sold for sex to visitors in the Dominican Republic's tourist towns. In April 2015 Dominican authorities, working with US Homeland Security Investigations, freed 29 victims, 20 of them aged 14 to 17, in the north-coast town of Sosúa and arrested seven Dominican nationals. US men have been prosecuted at home for abusing children on the north coast. The US State Department's 2025 report says teenage girls are often exploited on streets, in parks and on beaches, and charities link the growing number of child victims to weak regulation of tourism.

The cases against the two clergymen were decided in Poland and the Vatican, not in the country where the children lived. Exploitation of children in tourist areas continues.

story.story:
In March 2007 the British newspaper The Daily Telegraph described baby-buying, bribes and the deception of birth families in adoptions from Nepal. In April 2007 Nepal's new minister halted all intercountry adoptions. In November 2009, at the ministry's request, the Hague Conference on Private International Law, an intergovernmental body that writes treaties on family law including adoption, sent a mission to Nepal. Its report of February 2010 cited evidence that papers were regularly falsified to declare children adoptable, with false statements about abandonment, origin and age, and that this continued under new rules adopted in 2008. It said the US$5,000 payment for each child and the US$10,000 annual agency fee gave strong incentives unrelated to the cost of care. Nepal sent 1,991 children abroad for adoption between 2003 and 2022.

Inside Nepal, children's homes recruit children from poor families. In 2021/22 the National Child Rights Council counted 417 registered homes holding 10,905 children, and UNICEF estimates that about 85 percent have a living parent or guardian. Agents take money from rural families with promises of schooling and are paid commissions by the homes, and researchers say the homes use the children to attract donations. Only about 200 of 753 local governments had appointed the child welfare officers required by a 2018 law.

Girls are also taken across the open border to India. Nepal's National Human Rights Commission estimated that about 35,000 Nepalis were trafficked in 2018, including 5,000 children, and said poor screening at the border makes this hard to control. Traffickers recruit with offers of jobs or marriage and through online romance scams, and the 2025 US trafficking report raised serious concerns of official complicity. In 2015 police in Kolkata freed six young women trafficked from Nepal who all carried fake adult identity papers, which International Justice Mission, a charity that works with police, said traffickers issue to underage girls.

Adoption abroad was halted, and children are still moved into homes and across the border for money. Childlight found in 2026 that South Asia has no representative survey data on online exploitation of children.

story.story:
Gerald Ridsdale was ordained a Catholic priest in the Diocese of Ballarat, in Victoria, in 1961. By late 1975 his bishop, Ronald Mulkearns, knew that Ridsdale was abusing children, and kept moving him to new parishes and later to Sydney. Ridsdale was first convicted in 1993 and was eventually convicted of abusing more than 70 children.

In March 2008 the Adass Israel School, an ultra-Orthodox Jewish school in Melbourne, paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before police were told that she had abused pupils. Australia issued a warrant for 74 offences in 2014. In Israel the deputy health minister, Yaakov Litzman, pressured ministry staff to change psychiatric assessments so that she would appear unfit for extradition, the legal process of handing a suspect to another country. He later admitted breach of trust. Leifer was extradited in January 2021 and convicted in Melbourne in April 2023.

The Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse, a national public inquiry with the power to require documents, was announced in November 2012. Its final report in 2017 drew on 8,013 private sessions and evidence about 3,489 institutions; 58.1% of the survivors heard in private sessions had been abused in a religious institution and 32.5% in one run by the government. Its recommendations led to the National Redress Scheme, which began in 2018. Between 2015 and 2018 every state and territory removed or changed the limitation period, the legal deadline for suing over child abuse.

Australians also abused children abroad. In 2016 about 800 registered child sex offenders travelled overseas, often to developing countries in Asia, and 40% did not tell police. In 2020 the bank Westpac agreed to pay a A$1.3 billion penalty that included failing to check payments that could be linked to live-streamed abuse of children in the Philippines.

The Royal Commission counted abuse inside Australian institutions and led to changes in the law. Abuse paid for by Australians in other countries is known mainly through individual prosecutions and bank records.

story.story:
During the military dictatorship that ruled Argentina from 1976 to 1983, the armed and security forces held people in secret detention camps, and some of the women held there were pregnant. Their babies, and children kidnapped with their parents, were given to military families and allies of the regime and registered as those families' own children.

In 1977 the Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo was founded to find these children. Their work led to the creation of Argentina's National Bank of Genetic Data, which holds relatives' DNA for matching. In December 1983 President Raúl Alfonsín set up the National Commission on the Disappearance of Persons, known as CONADEP. Its 1984 report, Nunca Más, recorded 8,960 forced disappearances and at least 200 children under 15 kidnapped. In 2012 a federal court in Buenos Aires found that the junta, the ruling group of military commanders, had run a "systematic plan" to take children born to detained or disappeared mothers. It sentenced the former dictator Jorge Videla to 50 years and Reynaldo Bignone to 15. About 500 children are estimated to have been taken, and by July 2025 the Grandmothers had identified 140 of them.

The Italian priest Nicola Corradi had been accused at the Provolo school for deaf children in Verona in 2009 and flagged by the diocese there in 2011, and he went on working at the order's school in Luján de Cuyo, Mendoza. In 2019 a Mendoza court convicted him, the priest Horacio Corbacho and a gardener of abusing children there between 2004 and 2016, with sentences of 42, 45 and 18 years.

In Tucumán, a young woman was allegedly abducted in 2002 into forced prostitution by a brothel and trafficking network that also trafficked minors. The trial over her case ended in 2012 with all 13 defendants acquitted. The province's Supreme Court reversed this in 2013 and found 10 of them guilty. Campaigners and the family's lawyers said police were often paid to protect such networks.

Most of the children taken under the dictatorship have still not been identified, and the search for them continues through DNA matching.

story.story:
In 2003 Brazil's Congress set up a CPMI, a joint inquiry of senators and deputies, to investigate networks that sexually exploited children and adolescents. Its final report in July 2004 named more than 250 people, among them 20 serving politicians, including three mayors, about 30 businessmen and five priests, and passed their cases to prosecutors. Its draft rewrite of the Penal Code chapter on sexual crimes became law in 2009.

From 2008 to 2010 a Senate inquiry chaired by Senator Magno Malta examined abuse material shared online. It reached an agreement with Google, the Federal Police and prosecutors to open the records of pages on the Orkut social network linked to child abuse. Laws passed during its work made possessing abuse material a crime. A Pará state deputy, Luiz Afonso Sefer, whose fall Malta credited to the inquiry, was convicted in 2010 of raping a child; the case has since been overturned, reinstated and annulled on appeal, and as of February 2026 his 20-year sentence had not been carried out. In 2014 a Chamber of Deputies inquiry asked for 37 people to be indicted, among them Adail Pinheiro, the mayor of Coari in Amazonas, and a serving state deputy.

Much of the exploitation takes place along roads and in tourist towns. The Federal Highway Police's 2021–2022 survey of more than 9,700 truck stops, bars and motels rated 640 of them critical. The 2025 US State Department trafficking report says taxi drivers and hotel, bar and nightclub staff in northeastern coastal resorts help foreign offenders reach children, and that no investigations of complicit officials were reported.

Brazil has the largest Catholic population in the world, but no national inquiry into abuse in churches or children's institutions has been found. Cases have come out one at a time, as in Arapiraca in 2011, when a judge convicted three priests of abusing altar boys.

Three congressional inquiries named politicians and led to new laws, and the conviction of at least one of those politicians has still not been enforced. Abuse inside Brazil's institutions has never been counted nationally.

story.story:
The Holy See is both the central government of the Catholic Church and a state with its own diplomats and courts. In 1922, and again in 1962 in an instruction called Crimen sollicitationis, it ordered that church trials of priests accused of sexual acts with children be kept absolutely secret, on pain of automatic excommunication. In 2001 it required bishops to send every case of a cleric's sexual offence with a minor to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, its office for church discipline, and kept those cases under the pontifical secret, its highest level of confidentiality. Between 2004 and 2013 that office studied 3,420 credible cases and dismissed 884 priests from the priesthood.

In August 2013 it recalled Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, its nuncio, or ambassador, to the Dominican Republic, amid allegations that he had abused minors, before Dominican prosecutors opened their investigation. He was charged by a Vatican prosecutor in 2015 and died before trial. In 2017 it recalled Mgr Carlo Capella from its embassy in Washington, and in 2018 its own court convicted him of possessing and sharing child abuse images and sentenced him to five years; he was not tried in the United States or Canada. Archbishop Luigi Ventura, its nuncio to France, was tried in Paris in his absence and in December 2020 received an eight-month suspended sentence. Ireland's Murphy Commission, a state inquiry, received no files from the Vatican.

In 2014 the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child said the Holy See had placed the church's reputation and the protection of offenders above children's interests and had moved abusive priests to new parishes. In 2019 Pope Francis required clergy to report suspected abuse to church authorities, though not to the police, and in December 2019 he lifted the pontifical secret so that case files could be given to state authorities.

Since December 2019 church files on abuse can be given to state authorities, but the Holy See still decides whether to hand them over, and its own rules do not require clergy to report abuse to the police.

story.story:
In its final report, Chega!, published in 2005, Timor-Leste's Commission for Reception, Truth and Reconciliation found that at least 4,000 children had been forcibly taken from their families and moved illegally to Indonesia during the Indonesian occupation, which ended in 1999. Indonesian military units took children, some of whom they used as child soldiers or servants, and Islamic organisations took children and converted them. The children were often renamed and lost contact with their families. The commission and a joint Indonesia–Timor-Leste Commission of Truth and Friendship recommended a commission to search for the missing children, but it was never created.

Children from Indonesia were also sent abroad for adoption. In 2021 a Dutch commission of inquiry found serious violations in adoptions to the Netherlands from countries including Indonesia between 1967 and 1997/98, and the Dutch government suspended all intercountry adoption on 8 February 2021.

In July 2025 West Java police said a syndicate of recruiters, caretakers and document forgers had sold at least 25 babies since 2023, mostly to buyers in Singapore, for 11–16 million rupiah each, some 'reserved while still in the womb'. The syndicate prepared fraudulent family cards, the household registration document, and passports in Pontianak. Thirteen people were arrested, six babies were rescued, and police asked Interpol for help to trace the adopters.

The US State Department's 2025 report on trafficking says sexual exploitation of children by visiting foreigners is prevalent in the Riau Islands, which border Singapore, and that women and girls are coerced into commercial sex notably in Batam. It says tourists from the Middle East pay more than $700 for week-long 'contract marriages' in Puncak, Bogor, with girls as young as nine, a practice the government tacitly accepted, and that corruption and complicity significantly impeded efforts against trafficking.

In 2025 babies were still being sold abroad with forged papers, and foreign visitors were still paying for girls in the Riau Islands and Puncak. The children taken from Timor-Leste have never been searched for by the commission that was recommended.

story.story:
In 2004 a Norwegian government report, NOU 2004:23, examined municipal children's homes and state special schools between 1945 and 1980 and found neglect and abuse there, some of it serious and including sexual abuse. In 2005 a committee of the Storting, Norway's parliament, recommended that the state's compensation scheme pay up to NOK 300,000 and require a lower burden of proof.

Norway also took in children from abroad. Between 1955 and 2008 it received 6,295 children from South Korea, and in 1974 and 1975, when South Korea tried to stop sending children, Scandinavian diplomats pressed it to continue. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found that Korean agencies had sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign agencies' demand and had falsely registered children with known parents as orphans.

In 2023 Norway appointed a committee to investigate the adoptions. Its report, NOU 2026:7, presented in June 2026, examined adoptions from 12 countries since the 1950s and found illegal or unethical practices and clear failings in the Norwegian system throughout the period. It recorded a kidnapped child adopted to Norway, a mother told she would get money if she consented, and deliberately falsified documents. Payments to orphanages were sometimes linked to the number of children adopted. Norwegian adoption organisations did not always tell the authorities about payments or errors, and the authorities kept approving adoptions after learning of the risks.

In 2026, using a payment-tracing method developed the year before, Norwegian police helped police in seven countries arrest 28 men suspected of paying cryptocurrency for access to hidden online forums with abuse videos. After the US release of Jeffrey Epstein documents, the former prime minister Thorbjørn Jagland was charged in February 2026 with aggravated corruption over gifts, travel and loans. The case concerns corruption, not abuse, and he denies the charges.

Adopted people in Norway now have an official finding that the system that brought many of them there broke the law at times. In 2025 one Korean-born adoptee gave notice of a lawsuit against the state alleging that her adoption was illegal.

story.story:
Paul Schäfer, a former Nazi army corporal, fled a 1959 warrant in Siegburg, Germany, for abusing two boys, and in 1961 founded Colonia Dignidad, a closed German commune in southern Chile, where he drew children from local farms into the colony's free school and clinic. In 1966 a teenager who escaped took refuge at the West German embassy, which sent a delegation and said it found no evidence. Politicians rejected escapees' allegations because of the colony's ties to those preparing the 1973 coup. Chilean officials believe the Pinochet dictatorship later used the colony to torture its opponents. An investigation opened only after Chilean mothers complained in 1997, and in 2006 a Chilean court sentenced Schäfer to 20 years for abusing 25 children.

Under the dictatorship, from 1973 to 1990, adoptions of Chilean children abroad reached their peak. Babies were taken from mainly poor mothers, some of whom were told their babies had died, and sent to families in the United States and Europe. In 2018 a judge opened a criminal investigation covering about 8,000 adoptions abroad from 1970 to 1999. In 2019 a commission of the Chamber of Deputies, the lower house of Congress, found that hospital staff, Civil Registry staff and paid private intermediaries had taken part, and that some hospitals had destroyed birth records.

In the Catholic Church, parishioners reported the Santiago priest Fernando Karadima to the archbishop in 1984, and Cardinal Errázuriz shelved a credible church investigation in 2004–05. The Vatican found Karadima guilty of sexual abuse in 2011. In 2018, after receiving a 2,300-page report by his envoy, Pope Francis wrote that he had been mistaken, and every bishop in Chile offered to resign.

In 2012 family-court judges and UNICEF interviewed children in homes supervised by SENAME, the national child protection service, and found sexual abuse was a constant; in one home in Arica, carers ran a network that sexually exploited girls.

Courts and inquiries have now examined the colony, the church hierarchy and the state's care and adoption systems. As of September 2023 nobody had been brought to justice for the adoptions abroad.

story.story:
In 1971 Luis Fernando Figari founded the Sodalicio de Vida Cristiana, a Catholic lay society, in Lima. In 2015 the journalists Pedro Salinas and Paola Ugaz published a book describing abuse by Figari and those around him, and they then faced legal action. The Vatican appointed an official to examine the group the same year. In 2017 the society gave Peruvian prosecutors an expert report on sexual abuse of minors by Figari and four former members, and the Vatican barred him from contact with members. After a further Vatican investigation, Figari was expelled in August 2024 for physical, psychological and sexual violence, including against minors, and the society was formally dissolved in 2025.

Religious orders also moved abusers into and out of Peru. In 2010 Brother Abel Pérez of the Marist Brothers, a teaching order, confessed to his superiors in Chile that he had abused minors, and the order transferred him to Peru; in 2017 it acknowledged at least 14 victims. In the other direction, the Spanish Jesuit Alfonso Pedrajas first abused a child in Lima in 1964, then moved to Bolivia, where he abused more than 80 minors at Jesuit schools.

Children are also exploited in places where the state has little control. In 2019 more than 1,500 soldiers and police moved against illegal gold mining in La Pampa, in Madre de Dios, and the women's minister said child sexual exploitation had been among the worst crimes there. In 2021 a 16-year-old girl who had earlier been rescued from a trafficking group in La Pampa was found murdered. The US State Department reported in 2025 that tourists from the United States and Europe exploit children in Cusco, Lima and the Amazon, and that in Loreto criminal groups take tourists by boat to remote places on the river where women and children are exploited.

The Sodalicio no longer exists, and its founder has been expelled by the church but not convicted by a Peruvian court. Exploitation of children in mining camps and by tourists continues.

story.story:
In March 2008 the Adass Israel School, an ultra-Orthodox school in Melbourne, paid for its headmistress, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of allegations that she had abused pupils. Australia issued a warrant in 2014 for 74 offences. Her lawyers in Israel sought more than 70 hearings and appeals, and in 2019 she was found to have faked mental illness. The deputy health minister, Yaakov Litzman, had pressured ministry staff to change psychiatric evaluations so that she would appear unfit for extradition, the legal process of sending a suspect to another country for trial. Leifer was extradited in 2021 and convicted in Melbourne in 2023 of 18 charges including rape. Litzman admitted breach of trust in a plea deal, resigned from the Knesset, Israel's parliament, and received eight months' probation.

In June 2024 a UN Commission of Inquiry found that Israeli security forces had subjected Palestinians to sexual violence during arrests and in detention, that men and boys were targeted in particular ways, and that this amounted to gender persecution as a crime against humanity. It also found that sexual violence was committed in the attacks of 7 October 2023, when 36 children were among 252 people taken hostage.

Leifer was convicted in Australia in 2023 after years of hearings in Israel, and the minister who obstructed her extradition received probation.

story.story:
From the 1990s Russia sent large numbers of children from its orphanages to families abroad. The United States issued visas to 60,266 children adopted from Russia between 1994 and 2014, with the most, 5,865, in 2004.

In May 2000 Moscow police asked the US Customs Service for help with Blue Orchid, a Moscow-based website that sold videotapes of the sexual abuse of boys, some as young as 12, for $200 to $300 each, mostly mailed to customers in the United States. Russian police arrested the alleged operators in December 2000 and the site was shut in January 2001. By March 2001 four US citizens and five Russians had been arrested, and leads were passed to Sweden, Denmark and the Netherlands. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes abuse images, acted on 5,797 web addresses in Russia, 2 percent of its total.

After a criminal case was opened against him in St Petersburg in November 2013, the priest Gleb Grozovsky fled to Israel. He was detained and extradited to Russia, the legal process of sending a suspect back for trial, and in 2018 he was jailed for 14 years. After Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, a UN commission of inquiry found that Russian forces had raped Ukrainian children.

In the cases recorded here, offenders were caught when Russian and foreign police worked together or when a suspect who had fled abroad was sent back. No trial over the UN commission's finding that Russian forces raped children is recorded in the sources for this map.

story.story:
In April 1975 children were airlifted out of Vietnam in Operation Babylift, and a later lawsuit alleged that many of them were not orphans. Adoptions abroad continued in the following decades, and from 1994 to 2014 the United States alone issued 7,498 immigrant visas to children adopted from Hanoi, with a peak of 828 in 2007.

In April 2008 the US embassy in Hanoi reported that the number of babies recorded as abandoned had risen 17-fold or more at orphanages in seven provinces. Vietnam did not renew its adoption agreement with the United States when it expired that September. In 2009 a court in Nam Dinh tried 16 people, including the head of two social welfare centres and doctors and nurses at village clinics, for abuse of power. They were accused of asking poor families for their infants and falsifying documents to say the babies had been abandoned, and 266 babies were sent abroad for adoption between 2005 and 2008. Vietnam still sent 14,039 children abroad between 2003 and 2022, and in Belgium the Flemish government later stopped adoptions from Vietnam.

Foreigners also came to Vietnam to abuse children. In 2007 an Australian charity found 80 commercial cases of child exploitation by foreigners in Sa Pa, and the same year Vietnam set up a unit in the Ministry of Public Security to investigate child sex tourism. In 2006 a Vietnamese court had convicted the British singer Paul Gadd, known as Gary Glitter, of obscene acts with two girls aged 10 and 11.

Vietnamese children are also trafficked out of the country. The 2025 US State Department report on trafficking says traffickers in border villages lure women and girls, particularly Hmong, to China for forced marriages, and Vietnam identified 236 child victims in 2024. In Britain, 416 Vietnamese children were referred as potential victims of modern slavery that year, and Vietnamese children and adults there are exploited on cannabis farms and in nail salons.

Adoption from Vietnam has been cut back after the fraud cases. Vietnamese girls continue to be trafficked to China, and Vietnamese children to Britain.

story.story:
Between 2012 and 2015 the US-based group Disability Rights International investigated 33 Ukrainian orphanages, boarding schools and institutions for children with disabilities, and concluded that the orphanage system served traffickers as a way to recruit children. La Strada Ukraine, an anti-trafficking charity, told it that recruiting children from orphanages into prostitution was "the most typical scheme", and that sexual exploitation in institutions usually began around age 13, often started by staff. A coordinator for IOM, the UN migration agency, said most documented trafficking cases began in the vocational schools that orphanage leavers attend. Ukraine also sent 18,612 children abroad for adoption between 2003 and 2022, and the United States issued visas to 10,544 children adopted from Ukraine from 1994 to 2014.

After Russia's full invasion in February 2022, a UN commission of inquiry found that Russian forces had raped children. The war also put children left in Ukrainian institutions at risk. The US State Department's 2025 trafficking report said children evacuated from at least 195 facilities were at high risk, that officials at several state institutions were allegedly complicit or negligent, and that no complicit official had been convicted for the eighth year running.

Children who remain in Ukraine's institutions are at risk from traffickers, and no official has been convicted of taking part.

story.story:
China opened intercountry adoption, the adoption of its children by families abroad, in 1992. About 160,000 children were sent abroad, many to the United States, which issued 7,906 visas to children adopted from China in 2005 alone. Between 2002 and 2005 six state orphanages in Hunan province bought infants from traffickers who brought them from Guangdong and placed nearly 1,000 of them with families in China and abroad. In 2005 the authorities fired 23 officials, and three traffickers were sentenced to 15 years in prison. According to the New Yorker, the programme came to depend more and more on abuse, abduction and trafficking. On 5 September 2024 China's foreign ministry announced its end, except for adoption by blood relatives or of a stepchild.

Trafficking also runs in the other direction, bringing women and girls from neighbouring countries to be sold to Chinese men and families as brides. In 2019 Human Rights Watch documented women and girls from Kachin and northern Shan states in Myanmar, many displaced by war, who were sold to Chinese families for US$3,000 to 13,000, locked up and raped so they would become pregnant. In Pakistan, the Federal Investigation Agency listed 629 girls and women sold as brides to Chinese men from 2018 to mid-2019. Officials told the Associated Press that the investigation largely stopped after June 2019 because government officials feared harming relations with Beijing, and in October 2019 a court in Faisalabad acquitted 31 Chinese nationals after witnesses were threatened or bribed.

Little is known about online abuse of children inside China. In 2025 the US CyberTipline, which collects reports from technology companies, received 9,406 reports for China and 1,933,900 for India, because most US platforms are blocked in China.

The adoption programme has ended. The 2025 US reports say traffickers still take girls from Pakistan, Vietnam and Laos to China as brides, and that displaced girls in Myanmar remain at risk. The international records show almost nothing about online abuse of children inside China.

story.story:
For decades juvenile courts and social services in Tuscany placed children at Il Forteto, a farming cooperative and community at Vicchio near Florence. Its founder, Rodolfo Fiesoli, already had a final conviction in 1985, and the placements continued. He was later sentenced to 14 years and 10 months for abuse. A parliamentary inquiry did not reach a final report, and in 2024 parliament created a new commission of inquiry to establish why the authorities kept accrediting the community after court rulings on abuse.

In May 2012 the Italian Bishops' Conference, the body of Italy's Catholic bishops, said that under the Lateran concordat, the treaty between Italy and the Holy See, its priests had no obligation to report suspected abuse to the police. The priest Nicola Corradi, accused at the Provolo school for deaf children in Verona in 2009, went on working at the order's school in Argentina, where he was convicted in 2019.

From 2022 the bishops' conference began publishing its own national reports. Its first counted 86 contacts to diocesan listening centres in 2020 and 2021, and its third, in 2025, counted 115 alleged victims in 2023 and 2024. Critics, including the victims' group Rete l'Abuso, said the reports leave out court and Vatican cases. In 2025 a Munich law firm hired by the Diocese of Bolzano-Bressanone found 59 victims in 67 cases since 1964 and called the diocese's handling of cases until 2010 a systemic failure.

Italy is also the destination for women and girls trafficked from Edo State in Nigeria, overland through Niger and Libya and then by boat. The UN migration agency recorded an almost 600 percent rise in potential victims arriving by sea between 2014 and 2017. In 2016 Europol said 5,000 unaccompanied migrant children had disappeared after arriving in Italy, and that it had evidence some missing children in Europe had been sexually exploited.

Italy has held no national inquiry into abuse in its institutions as a whole, so the only national figures on church abuse are the ones the bishops publish about themselves.

story.story:
In its 2025 report on trafficking, the US State Department described how girls from rural Côte d'Ivoire and from other West African countries are brought to Abidjan, the largest city, by distant relatives who promise them school or training. Once there, the girls are made to work as servants in homes, where they are open to sexual exploitation. The report said Ivorian women and girls are trafficked for sex especially in Abidjan.

The same report described traffickers from Nigeria who recruit women and girls with offers of jobs in shops and then exploit them in the country's gold-mining and cocoa regions. The report on Nigeria said organised groups, some linked to Nigerian cult organisations, move women and girls to mining regions in several West African countries, Côte d'Ivoire among them.

Little else is counted. Childlight, a research centre that combines surveys into global estimates, found in 2026 that West and Central Africa had too few representative surveys on online exploitation of children to be measured.

The trafficking of girls into homes and mining areas is described in yearly US reports, and no national survey in this record measures how many children it affects.

story.story:
In 1964 the Spanish Jesuit priest Alfonso Pedrajas abused a child in Lima, Peru, and then settled in Bolivia, where he worked in Jesuit schools. In 1978 he confessed to a superior, who covered it up. In a diary published by the Spanish newspaper El País in 2023, Pedrajas, who died in 2009, wrote that he had abused at least 85 minors between 1972 and 2000. In May 2023 prosecutors seized internal Jesuit documents in La Paz and Cochabamba. On 2 September 2025 a Bolivian court sentenced Marcos Recolons and Ramón Alaix, former provincials, or heads of the Jesuits in Bolivia, to one year in prison each for knowing of allegations against Pedrajas and not reporting them. Sentences under three years are normally commuted in Bolivia, meaning replaced by a lighter penalty. Prosecutors said they would pursue other priests named at the trial.

Bolivia had about 150,000 Mennonites by 2023, many living in closed German-speaking farming colonies. Between 2005 and 2009, men in the Manitoba Colony sprayed a drug through bedroom windows to sedate families, then broke in and raped women and girls, including small children. The attacks were first blamed on ghosts or demons. After they came to light in June 2009, a Bolivian court in August 2011 convicted the men of raping and sexually assaulting 151 women and girls. A 2013 investigation reported similar assaults continuing.

In its 2025 report on trafficking, the US State Department said foreign offenders exploited children in rural Indigenous communities in northern La Paz department, in and around Rurrenabaque, and in tourist areas of La Paz and Beni. It said the production of abuse material for sale online was rising in Cochabamba, El Alto and Santa Cruz, and that Bolivian women and girls were exploited in sex trafficking in Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Panama and Peru.

The Jesuit superiors were convicted for failing to report, and prosecutors have said more priests may be charged. The abuse by foreign visitors and the abuse filmed for sale online are known mainly from a US government report.

story.story:
Between 2004 and 2007, soldiers of the Sri Lankan army contingent in MINUSTAH, the UN peacekeeping mission in Haiti, sexually exploited children in a ring that an Associated Press investigation later found involved at least 134 peacekeepers and at least nine children. In 2007 the UN Office of Internal Oversight Services, the UN's internal investigators, found that the abuse was frequent and took place at virtually every location where the contingent was deployed. Of the 950 Sri Lankan soldiers, 114 were accused and 108 were sent home. Only the country that sends a peacekeeper can prosecute them. Sri Lankan authorities judged the acts "consensual" and nobody was jailed; in 2016 one victim received a one-off ex gratia payment, a payment made without admitting liability.

Haiti also sent 13,986 children abroad for adoption between 2003 and 2022, and many children lived in orphanages paid for from abroad. In 2017 the charity Lumos found that at least US$70 million a year went to about a third of Haiti's orphanages, from donors 92 percent of whom were in the United States, and that only 15 percent of orphanages were registered. It found that these donations drove the opening of orphanages, some run purely for profit, which recruited children from their families. In 2007 a centre was forced to return 47 children awaiting adoption to their families, after misleading the parents with payments. In 2019 the government's social welfare agency, IBESR, assessed more than 750 orphanages and identified 3,019 potential victims of trafficking in them.

In 2024 the UN verified sexual violence against 566 children, 411 of them by the Viv Ansanm gang coalition, compared with 41 girls in 2023. The 2025 US trafficking report said many trafficked children are restavek, children sent to work unpaid as servants in other families' homes, and that displacement from Port-au-Prince increased their risk of sexual exploitation.

None of the peacekeepers who abused children was jailed. Children in Haiti now face sexual violence by gangs, unpaid servitude in other homes and an orphanage system kept going by foreign donations.

story.story:
In September 1995 Cardinal Hans Hermann Groër, the Archbishop of Vienna, stepped down after former pupils accused him of sexual abuse. In 1998 the Austrian bishops said they considered the allegations well founded. In 2010 abuse at the boarding school of Kremsmünster Abbey in Upper Austria became public, and in 2013 a court sentenced its former boarding director, to 12 years in prison for abusing 24 boys.

In spring 2010 the bishops set up the Independent Victims' Protection Commission, chaired by Waltraud Klasnic, to pay victims of church abuse. By 31 August 2021 payments had been approved in 2,550 cases, about €33 million in total.

Inquiries into homes run by cities and states followed. In 2013 a commission on the city's Wilhelminenberg home found that girls as young as about six had been raped and sexually exploited there by caregivers and outside men, and that city staff and politicians who knew of it in the 1960s did not act. From 2010 the city paid the victim-support organisation Weisser Ring to handle claims, and by 2019 it had paid 42.13 million euros to victims. In 2015 a University of Innsbruck study for the states of Tyrol and Vorarlberg found that their homes kept children isolated and dependent on staff, a system that produced and tolerated sexualised violence until the 1980s.

In October 2025, after reporting by the magazine Falter, the Austrian branch of the SOS Children's Villages charity said there were credible allegations that its founder, Hermann Gmeiner, who died in 1986, had abused eight boys between the 1950s and 1980s. Victims had come forward from 2013 and been compensated, but the charity had not made this public. Prosecutors in three cities opened investigations, and in 2026 a reform commission chaired by the former Supreme Court president Irmgard Griss examined the lack of outside oversight of the villages.

Most of the abuse found in Austria took place in church, city and state homes between 1945 and the 1990s, and has mainly led to compensation payments. The allegations against Gmeiner, kept inside the charity for years, are still under investigation.

story.story:
In 1991 the Catholic bishops of Malta set up a Response Team, chaired by Judge Victor Caruana Colombo, to deal with complaints of abuse by clergy. In April 2010 the Maltese Curia, the church's central administration, said the team had handled 45 cases of abuse of minors by priests over 19 years. Nineteen were dismissed as unfounded, 13 were still open, four priests had been found guilty and removed from ministry, and two priests had died. By the same month the church in Malta had recorded 84 allegations.

Some cases reached the criminal courts. Fr Charles Pulis was sentenced to six years and Fr Godwin Scerri to five years for abusing boys at St Joseph Home, a church children's home run by the Missionary Society of St Paul. Donald Bellizzi received three years in 2020.

Children from Malta were also sent abroad. Under child migration schemes, British and Maltese children were sent to institutions in Australia, among them homes run by the Christian Brothers, a Catholic religious order, at Bindoon, Castledare, Clontarf and Tardun in Western Australia. In August 2001 a committee of the Australian Senate reported that of 207 former child migrants who wrote to it, 38 described sexual abuse, 24 of them in Christian Brothers institutions in Western Australia. The committee described 'systemic criminal sexual assault' and predatory behaviour by a large number of Christian Brothers over a long period.

The figures on abuse by clergy in Malta come from the church's own Response Team and a few criminal convictions. The abuse of Maltese child migrants was examined in Australia, together with that of British children.

story.story:
In 1996 Thailand passed a law that made sex with anyone under 18 in a prostitution establishment a crime, whether or not the child agreed. The same year a Swiss man who had already been convicted of abusing children in Fribourg in 1980 and in Valais in 1991 returned to Thailand. Mainly between 2002 and 2013 he abused more than 80 boys in Pattaya, where he ran a bar with a hotel room used by European men, and in Nong Hoi in the north, and he forced boys to perform sexual acts with European clients. He was tried in Switzerland, and on 1 March 2018 a Swiss court sentenced him to 16 years. Between 2011 and 2013 the British former teacher and scout leader Mark Frost abused boys from poor families in Thailand. In February 2017 he was sentenced in Britain to 13 life terms after pleading guilty to 45 offences there and in Thailand.

Thailand passed its Anti-Human Trafficking Act in 2008, and in 2017 it refused entry to 74 known foreign sex offenders. Abuse of Thai children was also sold online. In 2017 Interpol, the international police organisation, found material showing the abuse of 11 boys under 13, published weekly on a subscription website on the dark web with nearly 63,000 users. Its main administrator, in Thailand, was arrested in January 2018, and in June 2018 a Thai court sentenced him to 146 years. Interpol said 50 children had been removed from harm.

In 2023 police raided an illegal bar on Bangla Road in Patong, Phuket, and rescued six children under 18 who were being sexually exploited there. Five senior Patong police officers were transferred to other posts after the raid. On 19 July 2024 the Phuket Provincial Court sentenced seven Thai and foreign defendants, and the owner received a total of 1,073 years.

Thai courts now give very long sentences to the offenders they convict. The US State Department's 2025 report on trafficking says children from Thailand, Burma, Cambodia and Laos are increasingly sold for sex in brothels, bars, karaoke lounges and hotels in Thailand.
